MAPBig-picture map of prenatal testing

LO 1Screening vs diagnostic tests

Q1. Why do prenatal genetic testing at all?
  • Reassurance for families at risk
  • Preparation for the birth of an affected baby, and for the timing and mode of delivery
  • Risk information for couples for whom termination is an option
  • In the near future: treatment in utero (stem-cell or gene therapy)
Q2. How is a screening test different from a diagnostic test?

Screening

  • Examines low-risk individuals to find those at high risk
  • Typically inexpensive and non-invasive (blood, ultrasound)
  • Result = a risk, not an answer

Diagnosis

  • Determines whether disease is present in a high-risk population
  • Usually invasive (amniocentesis, CVS)
  • Result = yes or no

ACOG recommends offering both screening and diagnostic tests to all pregnant women, out of respect for patient autonomy.

In-house exam

Screening = low-risk population, non-invasive, cost-effective. Diagnosis = confirms disease in people already identified as high risk (by screening, family history or other factors).

Analogy — the smoke detector and the firefighter

A screen is a smoke detector: cheap, in every house, and sometimes it goes off for burnt toast. A diagnostic test is the firefighter who comes in and checks for an actual fire.

Q3. Which patients choose screening?

The patient's attitude is the most important determinant of whether she takes up screening.

TypeAttitudeWhat she wants
AnxiousHigh anxietyTesting irrespective of risk (goes straight to diagnosis)
BalanceWeighs risksA risk estimate before considering invasive testing → best candidate for screening
ContentDeclinesRefuses both screening and diagnosis
Memory tool

A-B-C: Anxious wants it all, Balance wants the screen, Content wants nothing.

Q4. How do I describe a screen's accuracy?
AffectedNormal
Test abnormalaca + c
Test normalbdb + d
a + bc + d
MeasureFormulaMeaning
Detection rate (= sensitivity)a / (a + b)Affected fetuses the screen catches
False-positive ratec / (c + d)Normal fetuses falsely flagged
Positive predictive valuea / (a + c)Chance a positive screen is truly affected
Negative predictive valued / (b + d)Chance a negative screen is truly normal

Detection and false-positive rates must be translated into predictive values: that's what the patient actually needs to know.

Trap

Detection rate and FPR describe the test; PPV depends on the prevalence too. A near-perfect test can still have a modest PPV when the disease is rare.

Q5. Why can a 99% detection rate give a PPV of only 66%?
  • With detection ≈100%, one false positive among 998 normals still makes up a third of all positives
High yield

When a patient gets a result, what matters is the chance it's correct: PPV for a positive, NPV for a negative. A positive screen always needs diagnostic confirmation.

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A screen catches 95 of 100 affected fetuses and flags 50 of 10,000 normal ones. Detection rate, FPR and PPV?
Detection 95%; FPR 50/10,000 = 0.5%; PPV 95/(95 + 50) ≈ 66%.
A2A patient weighs her risk carefully and wants numbers before deciding on amniocentesis. Which type is she?
Type Balance: the best candidate for a screening test.

LO 2DNA vs non-DNA screening

Q1. How do non-DNA screens find single-gene disorders?
  • Family history of an affected individual
  • Family history of female infertility, premature ovarian failure, unexplained intellectual disability, developmental delay or autism → risk factors for Fragile X
  • Ethnicity (ACOG): all ethnicities → SMA and CF; Ashkenazi Jewish → a panel that includes Tay-Sachs
Step 1

Fragile X premutation carriers (55–200 CGG repeats) get premature ovarian insufficiency (women) and FXTAS (older men); full mutation (>200) → intellectual disability, autism, macroorchidism.

Q2. What does an NGS expanded carrier screen add?
  • Done pre-conception or early in pregnancy on saliva or blood from both parents
  • Screens for >100 single-gene disorders; applicable to all ethnic groups
  • Both parents carriers for the same AR condition → 25% risk of an affected fetus → offer invasive diagnosis
  • Detects 3× as many carriers as ethnicity-based screening; outperforms it across every racial/ethnic group
  • 24% of individuals carry at least one non-mild condition, but <1% of couples carry the same one
  • Ethnicity misleads: ≈½ of Tay-Sachs carriers had no Jewish ancestry; many "ethnic" disorders are widely distributed
Ideal panel condition (ACOG / ACMG)
Carrier frequency ≥1:100
Well-defined phenotype; severe
Early-childhood onset
Detection rate ≥70%
Detrimental effect on quality of life: cognitive or physical impairment, need for surgical or medical intervention

Only 27% of conditions on commercial panels meet these criteria.

High yield

Expanded carrier screening beats ethnicity-based screening. A Tay-Sachs carrier may have no Jewish ancestry.

Trap

A carrier screen tests the parents, not the fetus. Two carrier parents still need diagnostic testing of the fetus (or PGT) to know whether this pregnancy is affected.

Q3. Which chromosome anomalies are found most often?
  • 71% of prenatally diagnosed anomalies are trisomy 21 (≈53%), 18 (≈13%) and 13 (≈5%)

Chromosome anomalies diagnosed prenatally

  • T21 + T18 + T13 = 71%
Q4. What are the non-DNA screens for aneuploidy?
ScreenKey points
Family historyPrior child with a chromosome anomaly; parent carrying a balanced translocation
Maternal ageTrisomy risk rises sharply after 35, but ≈55% of Down syndrome births are to women under 35 (because most births are) → don't screen by age alone
Maternal serum markers (1st or 2nd trimester)Proteins made by the fetus and/or placenta; aneuploid pregnancies have different levels
Sonographic markersNuchal translucency (fluid behind the fetal neck) in the 1st trimester

Maternal age

  • Risk climbs after 35, yet 55% of DS births are under 35

Nuchal translucency

  • ↑ thickness → ↑ aneuploidy risk

Why it's only a screen

  • Curves overlap: NT alone DR ≈55% at 5% FPR
Step 1 — serum marker patterns
Condition1st trimesterQuad screen (2nd trimester)
Trisomy 21↓ PAPP-A, ↑ β-hCG, ↑ NT↓ AFP, ↑ hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin A
Trisomy 18↓ PAPP-A, ↓ β-hCG, ↑ NT↓ AFP, ↓ hCG, ↓ estriol, nl/↓ inhibin A
Trisomy 13↓ PAPP-A, ↓ β-hCG, ↑ NT—
Neural tube defect—↑ AFP (+ ↑ amniotic AChE)

"HIgh" in Down syndrome: hCG and Inhibin go up; everything else goes down.

Q5. How does cell-free DNA screening work?
  • Maternal cfDNA comes from normal cell turnover; fetal cfDNA comes from placental apoptosis
  • Fetal DNA ≈ 10% of total cfDNA; cleared from maternal blood within hours of birth
  • Sequencing assigns each fragment to its chromosome; an excess of chr21 fragments → trisomy 21

Cell-free DNA

  • Placental fragments mix with maternal DNA

Counting fragments

  • A small excess of chr21 = T21
ConditionDetection rateFalse-positive ratePPV (age 30)
Trisomy 21>99%0.2%58%
Trisomy 1897%0.4%19%
Trisomy 1388%<1%13%
Monosomy X95%1%—

Screens for Down syndrome over time

  • Non-DNA screens at 5% FPR; cfDNA ≈99% at ≤0.1% FPR
High yield — false-positive cfDNA
  • Placental (confined) mosaicism: the DNA is placental, not fetal
  • Vanishing twin with an abnormal karyotype
  • Maternal mosaicism (e.g., age-related X loss in women >40 → false Turner)
  • Maternal transplant or tumor
Trap

cfDNA is a screen, not a diagnosis. Even with >99% detection, a positive T13 result in a 30-year-old is correct only 13% of the time → confirm with amniocentesis.

Memory tool

PPVs fall as the trisomy gets rarer: 21 → 58%, 18 → 19%, 13 → 13% ("13 for 13").

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A cfDNA screen shows monosomy X, but amniocentesis shows 46,XX. The mother is 42. Likely explanation?
Maternal mosaicism (age-related X loss in maternal cells), or placental mosaicism.
A2A woman with no Jewish ancestry asks whether she needs Tay-Sachs screening. What does the expanded-panel data say?
About half of Tay-Sachs carriers on expanded panels had no Jewish ancestry; ethnicity is a poor predictor.

LO 3Prenatal diagnosis: indications, methods, lab studies

Q1. When is prenatal diagnosis indicated?
#IndicationNote
1A parent with a structural chromosome abnormality (e.g., balanced translocation)Fetal risk depends on the type of anomaly and the parent of origin
2Previous child with a de novo aneuploidyRecurrence risk for any chromosome abnormality ≈1/100
3Genetic disorder amenable to prenatal diagnosisRisk from family history, positive screen (single gene or aneuploidy) or ultrasound findings
4Maternal desire to rule out genetic conditionsOffered even when risk is low
Step 1

≈95% of Down syndrome is meiotic nondisjunction (sporadic; risk rises with maternal age), ≈4% Robertsonian translocation (higher recurrence if a parent carries it), ≈1–2% mosaic.

Q2. How do amniocentesis, CVS and PGT compare?
AmniocentesisCVSPGT
SampleAmniotic fluid → fetal cells (skin, urinary tract)Biopsy of chorion frondosumBlastomere or 5–8 trophectoderm cells from a blastocyst
Timing / route2nd trimester; needle under ultrasound10–14 weeks; transcervical or transabdominalBefore implantation; requires IVF
Fetal loss above background1/300–1/500 (background 1–2%)0.2–0.3% (background 2–5%)Biopsy: no ↑ anomalies or adverse outcome to 5 years
AdvantageGold standard; confirms ambiguous CVS/PGTEarly resultsSelect unaffected embryos
DrawbackRare: feto-maternal hemorrhage, fluid leak, infectionAmbiguous in ≈1% from placental mosaicism → needs amnioIVF cost and risks; embryo mosaicism; false results 2–5%

Amniocentesis

  • Needle into the amniotic sac; aspirate fluid

CVS

  • Transabdominal (left) or transcervical (right)

PGT biopsy

  • Day 3 blastomere or day 5–6 trophectoderm
Memory tool

CVS = Chorion, Confusing (mosaic), Come early. Amnio = Answer (the confirmatory test).

Step 1

Amniocentesis is typically done at 15–20 weeks; CVS before 10 weeks has been linked to limb-reduction defects. Amniotic fluid also allows AFP/AChE for neural tube defects.

Trap

An abnormal cell line seen on CVS may be limited to the placenta (confined placental mosaicism). Confirm with amniocentesis before acting on it.

Q3. What are the indications, issues and errors of PGT?

Indications

  • Single-gene disorder when both parents are carriers (also HLA matching)
  • Structural rearrangement in a couple with a balanced translocation
  • Screening for de novo aneuploidy

Issues

  • Requires IVF: expensive, intrusive, ovarian hyperstimulation, multiples, adverse outcomes
  • Extended culture: 50% of embryos survive to day 3, 25% to day 8; lower implantation after day 6; monozygotic twins with late transfer
ErrorCauseConsequence
False negativeContaminating DNA, allele drop-out (failure to amplify), partial amplificationAbnormal embryo transferred
MisdiagnosisUnprotected sex during IVF, human error (wrong embryo), post-zygotic mitotic changes—
False positiveEmbryo mosaicism (16%)Normal or "self-correcting" mosaic embryos discarded; up to 30% embryo wastage
  • Quoted FP/FN risk 2–5%; the value of PGT for aneuploidy "has yet to be determined"
  • Confirm PGT diagnostic results with CVS or (preferred) amniocentesis; continue routine prenatal screening
Trap

Mosaic embryos with 20–50% abnormal cells can still produce healthy children. A "positive" PGT doesn't always mean an affected baby.

Q4. Which lab study do I run on the sample?
StudyUseKey numbers
KaryotypeTraditional standard for aneuploidy and gross rearrangements; used when the indication is a specific aneuploidy or an unbalanced translocation10–14 days; FISH quick result in 48–72 h
Chromosomal microarrayFetus with structural anomalies on ultrasound; fetal death needing genetic work-up. Without anomalies, karyotype or microarray may be offered5–10% extra yield when karyotype is normal
Prenatal exome sequencingMultiple anomalies with normal karyotype and microarray; a single major anomaly or pattern suggesting a genetic disorder; prior undiagnosed affected fetus/child/stillborn20–30% diagnostic yield
In-house exam

Prenatal exome sequencing: ultrasound shows multiple anomalies and karyotype + microarray are normal. It finds single-gene disorders the other tests miss.

High yield

Microarray and exome need pre- and post-test counseling: variants of uncertain significance (CNVs), non-paternity or consanguinity (SNP arrays), incidental/secondary findings, and re-analysis over time.

Q5. What's coming next?
  • cfDNA (NIPT) screening beyond T21/18/13: monosomy X, trisomy 9, unbalanced translocations, large deletions (low PPVs)
  • cfDNA diagnosis of single-gene disorders, already reported:
InheritanceDisorders
ADMyotonic dystrophy, early-onset primary dystonia, Huntington disease, achondroplasia, Apert, thanatophoric dysplasia, Crouzon
ARCystic fibrosis, propionic acidemia, Leber congenital amaurosis, sickle cell, β-thalassemia
X-linkedHemophilia A and B

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1CVS at 11 weeks shows 47,XX,+16 in some cells. Next step?
Amniocentesis: likely confined placental mosaicism; confirm the fetal karyotype.
A2Ultrasound shows heart, kidney and limb anomalies; karyotype and microarray are normal. Next test?
Prenatal exome sequencing (20–30% yield).
A3A couple's first child had de novo trisomy 21. Recurrence risk for any chromosome abnormality?
≈1/100 → offer prenatal diagnosis.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1Which statement best describes a prenatal screening test?

Screening finds who is at high risk; diagnosis confirms.

2A screen for T21 (prevalence 1 in 500) has 99% detection and 0.1% false positives. In 1,000 women, what is its positive predictive value?

2 true positives + 1 false positive → 2/3.

3Which patient attitude makes someone the best candidate for a screening test?

Balance wants a risk estimate before deciding on invasive testing.

4A woman's family includes several women with premature ovarian failure and a nephew with autism. Which disorder should be screened for?

Infertility, POF, unexplained ID, developmental delay or autism → Fragile X risk.

5Compared with ethnicity-based screening, NGS expanded carrier screening:

Saliva/blood from both parents; >100 disorders; 3× the carriers.

6Both parents are carriers for the same autosomal recessive disorder on expanded screening. What is the risk to each pregnancy, and what is offered?

AR × AR → 25% affected → offer CVS/amnio (or PGT).

7Fetal cell-free DNA in maternal blood comes mainly from:

Fetal cfDNA = placental apoptosis (≈10% of total); maternal cfDNA = normal turnover.

8A cfDNA screen is positive for trisomy 18, but amniocentesis shows a normal karyotype. Which is the most likely reason?

cfDNA is placental; placental mosaicism (or vanishing twin) causes false positives.

9What is the main advantage of CVS over amniocentesis?

CVS at 10–14 weeks; drawback: ≈1% ambiguous (placental mosaicism).

10The in-house risk of fetal loss attributable to amniocentesis is closest to:

1/300–1/500 above a background loss of 1–2%.

11A fetus has multiple structural anomalies. Karyotype and chromosomal microarray are normal. Best next test?

Exome sequencing: 20–30% yield in this setting.

12A couple uses PGT and discards an embryo reported as aneuploid. Which phenomenon most often makes such a result a false positive?

Mosaicism (16% of embryos) → false positives; allele drop-out → false negatives.
